title: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)
short_description: Enforces transport encryption using TLS to protect data in transit between the client browser and web server.
what_is_it: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS/SSL) encrypts the standard HTTP communication channel using symmetric encryption negotiated during a TLS handshake. It provides three essential guarantees: confidentiality (eavesdroppers cannot read traffic), integrity (data cannot be altered in transit), and authentication (proves the user is communicating with the intended server).
why_it_matters: Without HTTPS, every byte of web traffic travels in cleartext across local networks, ISP routers, and international transit backbones. Passwords, session cookies, personal identity details, and financial data can be trivially intercepted by anyone on the network path using tools like Wireshark.
actual_problem: When a site serves content over plaintext HTTP, attackers on the same network (such as public Wi-Fi hotspots) can execute Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. They can sniff credentials, inject malicious JavaScript advertisements, forge downloads, or hijack active user sessions via packet inspection and ARP spoofing.
security_impact: Loss of session confidentiality, credential theft, passive network eavesdropping, and arbitrary content injection directly into the user's browser viewport.
how_to_check: Inspect the URL scheme in the browser address bar (must start with 'https://' with a lock icon). Alternatively, run 'curl -I https://yourdomain.com' to verify that port 443 answers with a valid TLS handshake and appropriate HTTP response codes.

how_to_fix.overview: Obtain a trusted SSL/TLS certificate (such as a free Let's Encrypt automated certificate via Certbot) and configure your web server to bind to port 443 with TLS enabled.
how_to_fix.apache:
# /etc/apache2/sites-available/default-ssl.conf
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName example.com
    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/cert.pem
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem
    SSLCertificateChainFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/chain.pem
</VirtualHost>
how_to_fix.flask:
# For production, use Gunicorn or Nginx reverse proxy. For local testing:
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(ssl_context=('cert.pem', 'key.pem'), port=443)

example.good: https://example.com/login (Traffic encrypted with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305)
example.bad: http://example.com/login (Credentials sent in plaintext ASCII over TCP port 80)

common_mistakes: Allowing mixed content where the HTML loads over HTTPS but scripts or images load over HTTP.
Failing to redirect plaintext HTTP (port 80) traffic to HTTPS (port 443) automatically.
Using self-signed certificates in production, causing severe browser trust warning screens.
Forgetting to renew certificates before the 90-day validity window closes.

status_meanings.PASS: Website is accessible over HTTPS with a valid TLS connection.
status_meanings.MISSING: Website does not respond over HTTPS or refuses secure port 443 connections.
status_meanings.WARNING: HTTPS is supported but has connection quirks or fallback issues.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Website requires manual verification of internal endpoint routing.

title: SSL/TLS Protocol Configuration
short_description: Validates that the server supports modern, secure cryptographic protocols (TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3) and disallows obsolete protocols (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1).
what_is_it: Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the cryptographic protocol that succeeded Secure Sockets Layer (SSL). Modern web security mandates TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3. Legacy protocols (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1) and broken cipher suites (such as RC4, 3DES, or CBC-mode ciphers without Encrypt-then-MAC) are structurally vulnerable.
why_it_matters: Outdated protocols suffer from fatal protocol flaws such as POODLE (SSLv3), BEAST (TLS 1.0), and SWEET32 (Triple-DES). Attackers can force protocol downgrade attacks, decrypt session keys, or inject plaintext into supposedly encrypted connections.
actual_problem: If the web server enables backwards compatibility with ancient SSL/TLS protocols, attackers can exploit cipher downgrade vulnerabilities during the TLS ClientHello/ServerHello negotiation phase, compromising session secrecy.
security_impact: Decryption of recorded TLS network sessions, Man-in-the-Middle downgrade attacks, and non-compliance with standards like PCI-DSS and NIST SP 800-52.
how_to_check: Connect via OpenSSL CLI: 'openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3' or '-tls1_2' to check protocol negotiation. Test against obsolete versions like '-tls1_1' to ensure the server rejects them.

how_to_fix.overview: Explicitly restrict server TLS protocols to TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3 in your server configuration and employ forward-secret AEAD cipher suites.
how_to_fix.apache:
# In ssl.conf
SSLProtocol all -SSLv3 -TLSv1 -TLSv1.1
SSLCipherSuite HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5:!3DES:!CAMELLIA:!RC4
SSLHonorCipherOrder on
how_to_fix.flask: # In Flask production, handle TLS at the reverse proxy (Nginx/HAProxy/Traefik).

example.good: Server accepts only TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3 with forward-secret AEAD ciphers (GCM/Poly1305).
example.bad: Server negotiates TLSv1.0 or accepts 3DES (Triple DES) or RC4 cipher suites.

common_mistakes: Leaving default legacy OS cipher lists enabled without overriding ssl_protocols.
Disabling TLS 1.3 because of perceived incompatibility with legacy clients.
Using static RSA key exchange which lacks Forward Secrecy (PFS).

references.title: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2: Guidelines for TLS Implementations
OWASP Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet

status_meanings.PASS: Server successfully negotiated TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 with strong modern ciphers.
status_meanings.MISSING: Server does not support modern TLS versions.
status_meanings.WARNING: Server supports TLS 1.2 but does not yet enable TLS 1.3, or supports weak legacy ciphers.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Custom handshake constraints prevented full automated cipher suite enumeration.

title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
short_description: Tells browsers to always interact with the website exclusively over HTTPS, preventing SSL-stripping attacks.
what_is_it: HSTS is an HTTP response header defined in RFC 6797. When sent by a server over HTTPS, it instructs compliant web browsers that the site must never be loaded over insecure HTTP for a declared duration ('max-age'). It also forbids users from bypassing SSL certificate warning dialogs.
why_it_matters: Even if a server redirects HTTP to HTTPS, the very first request a user makes is often over unencrypted HTTP (e.g. typing 'example.com' into the address bar). A local attacker can intercept this initial request and execute an SSL-stripping attack (like sslstrip), preventing the browser from ever transitioning to HTTPS.
actual_problem: Without HSTS, the initial plaintext HTTP request is vulnerable to interception and downgrade. Furthermore, if an attacker presents a fraudulent certificate, non-HSTS browsers allow the user to click 'Proceed anyway', making phishing and MitM trivial.
security_impact: Vulnerability to SSL-stripping, interception of initial authentication requests, and user bypass of certificate errors under active attack.
how_to_check: Run 'curl -I https://example.com' and look for the 'Strict-Transport-Security' header. Check that 'max-age' is at least 15724800 (6 months) or 31536000 (1 year), and evaluate if 'includeSubDomains' and 'preload' are present.

how_to_fix.overview: Add the Strict-Transport-Security response header with a long max-age. Once verified across all subdomains, consider appending includeSubDomains and submitting to the HSTS Preload list (hstspreload.org).
how_to_fix.nginx:
# In your HTTPS server block
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload" always;
how_to_fix.apache:
# In your VirtualHost *:443 block
Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload"

example.good: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
example.bad: Header completely absent, or max-age=0 (which immediately deletes HSTS cache).

common_mistakes: Sending HSTS over unencrypted HTTP responses (RFC 6797 specifies browsers must ignore HSTS over HTTP).
Setting max-age too low (e.g., 300 seconds), defeating the long-term caching intent.
Adding 'includeSubDomains' before ensuring that internal subdomains (e.g., dev, mail, wiki) support HTTPS.

status_meanings.PASS: Strict-Transport-Security header is present with a recommended max-age (>= 180 days).
status_meanings.MISSING: Header is missing entirely, leaving users exposed to SSL-stripping.
status_meanings.WARNING: Header is present, but max-age is under 6 months, or lacks includeSubDomains.
status_meanings.REVIEW: HSTS header detected with unusual syntax or preload parameters requiring policy review.

title: Content Security Policy (CSP)
short_description: Restricts sources from which scripts, styles, images, and other assets can be executed, serving as the primary defense against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
what_is_it: Content Security Policy (CSP Level 3) is a declarative HTTP response header that lets server administrators define trusted origins for web assets (scripts, stylesheets, frames, fonts, web workers, connect endpoints). It drastically restricts the execution of injected malicious scripts.
why_it_matters: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) remains one of the most common and damaging web vulnerabilities. If an attacker manages to reflect or store malicious JavaScript, CSP prevents the browser from executing that script unless it originates from an authorized source or matches a cryptographic nonce/hash.
actual_problem: In the absence of a Content-Security-Policy header, browsers execute any script encountered in the DOM or fetched from arbitrary third-party domains, enabling attackers to steal auth tokens, keylog form entries, and deface pages.
security_impact: Execution of arbitrary injected client-side code, credential extraction from DOM storage, session hijacking, and drive-by malware delivery.
how_to_check: Inspect response headers for 'Content-Security-Policy'. Check whether 'default-src' or 'script-src' is defined and verify that insecure keywords like 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' are omitted or guarded by nonces.

how_to_fix.overview: Implement a restrictive CSP starting with default-src 'self'. Whitelist only required CDN domains, and adopt nonce-based or hash-based script authentication.
how_to_fix.nginx: add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted-cdn.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none';" always;
how_to_fix.apache: Header set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none';"

example.good: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-rAnd0m'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self';
example.bad: Content-Security-Policy: default-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' (effectively disables protection).

common_mistakes: Using 'unsafe-inline' in script-src without a nonce or hash, which nullifies anti-XSS safeguards.
Using wildcard '*' origins for script-src or connect-src.
Forgetting 'object-src 'none'', allowing Flash/Java plugin exploitation on older systems.
Failing to define 'frame-ancestors', leaving the site open to framing.

references.title: OWASP Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet

status_meanings.PASS: Content-Security-Policy header is configured with robust origin restrictions.
status_meanings.MISSING: Header is completely missing, leaving no browser-enforced asset boundary.
status_meanings.WARNING: Header is present but contains permissive directives like 'unsafe-inline' or wildcard '*'.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only is active or complex policy requires site-specific audit.

title: X-Content-Type-Options
short_description: Instructs the browser to strictly adhere to the MIME type declared in the Content-Type header, blocking MIME-sniffing attacks.
what_is_it: X-Content-Type-Options is an HTTP response header that takes a single canonical directive: 'nosniff'. When present, it disables the browser's MIME-type sniffing behavior, forcing it to render the payload strictly according to the server's Content-Type declaration.
why_it_matters: Browsers historically inspected file contents ('sniffed' the binary stream) to guess the type if they believed the server mislabeled it. An attacker could upload a harmless-looking file (e.g. an image containing executable JavaScript or HTML) and trick the browser into executing it as script.
actual_problem: If a user uploads an avatar file with an image extension (.png) but containing valid HTML/JS, a browser with MIME sniffing enabled might treat it as text/html when viewed directly, resulting in Stored Cross-Site Scripting.
security_impact: Execution of untrusted script payloads disguised as benign binary or text media (MIME confusion / polyglot attacks).
how_to_check: Verify that responses include the header 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff'.

how_to_fix.overview: Set the response header 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' across all server responses.
how_to_fix.nginx: add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
how_to_fix.apache: Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
how_to_fix.express:
const helmet = require('helmet');
app.use(helmet.noSniff());

example.good: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
example.bad: Header absent, or set to an invalid value.

common_mistakes: Serving stylesheets or scripts with improper Content-Type headers (e.g., text/plain) while 'nosniff' is active, causing the browser to legitimately block the asset.
Omitting the header on user-uploaded file download endpoints.

status_meanings.PASS: X-Content-Type-Options is correctly configured with 'nosniff'.
status_meanings.MISSING: Header is missing, enabling browser MIME-sniffing behavior.
status_meanings.WARNING: Header is set to a non-standard or malformed value.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Header present on dynamic endpoints but verify static asset configurations.

title: X-Frame-Options (Clickjacking Protection)
short_description: Controls whether a web page can be rendered inside an <iframe>, <frame>, <embed>, or <object>, mitigating clickjacking attacks.
what_is_it: X-Frame-Options is a legacy yet universally supported HTTP response header designed to prevent clickjacking (UI redressing). It can be configured with 'DENY' (prevents any domain from framing the site) or 'SAMEORIGIN' (allows framing only by pages from the exact same origin). In modern standards, it is complemented by CSP's 'frame-ancestors' directive.
why_it_matters: In a clickjacking attack, an adversary embeds your authenticated website inside a transparent iframe overlay on their malicious website. When the victim clicks an attractive button on the outer site, their click actually lands on an action button (such as 'Delete Account' or 'Transfer Funds') within your framed application.
actual_problem: Websites without framing restrictions allow attackers to weaponize user trust by invisibly overlaying their sensitive interactive forms inside third-party pages.
security_impact: Unauthorized state changes, financial transactions, permission grants, or account takeovers executed inadvertently by authenticated victims.
how_to_check: Look for 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' or 'SAMEORIGIN' in HTTP headers, or verify that CSP includes 'frame-ancestors 'none'' or 'frame-ancestors 'self''.

how_to_fix.overview: Configure X-Frame-Options to DENY or SAMEORIGIN, and pair it with CSP frame-ancestors for modern multi-layer defense.
how_to_fix.nginx:
add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
# Or SAMEORIGIN if framing within the same domain is required
how_to_fix.apache: Header always set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
how_to_fix.express:
const helmet = require('helmet');
app.use(helmet.frameguard({ action: 'deny' }));

example.good: X-Frame-Options: DENY (or SAMEORIGIN)
example.bad: Header missing, or obsolete 'ALLOW-FROM uri' used (deprecated in modern browsers).

common_mistakes: Using 'ALLOW-FROM', which is obsolete and ignored by modern browsers; use CSP 'frame-ancestors' instead.
Applying DENY to pages that legitimately need to be embedded in trusted enterprise portals without configuring CSP frame-ancestors.
Forgetting to set the header on authentication, password reset, and settings pages.

status_meanings.PASS: X-Frame-Options is set to DENY or SAMEORIGIN (or covered by CSP frame-ancestors).
status_meanings.MISSING: Header is missing and no CSP frame-ancestors is present.
status_meanings.WARNING: Header is configured with obsolete directives like ALLOW-FROM.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Framing allowed under custom CSP frame-ancestors policy; verify trusted whitelist.

title: Referrer-Policy
short_description: Governs how much sensitive referrer information (full URL path, query string) is sent in the Referer header when navigating between pages.
what_is_it: The Referrer-Policy header controls how the browser populates the 'Referer' header during outgoing HTTP requests triggered by links, images, or AJAX calls. Secure policies include 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' and 'no-referrer'.
why_it_matters: Web URLs often inadvertently contain sensitive information in their query strings—such as password reset tokens, session tokens, user IDs, internal document identifiers, or search parameters. When an unconfigured site links to an external service (or loads third-party scripts/images), that entire URL is transmitted to the third party in the Referer header.
actual_problem: Leaking private query parameters to third-party CDNs, analytics providers, or external hyperlinks, exposing credentials and violating user privacy.
security_impact: Exposure of sensitive query parameters, secret token leakage, PII disclosure, and unintended user tracking.
how_to_check: Inspect response headers for 'Referrer-Policy'. Common recommended values: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin', 'same-origin', or 'no-referrer'.

how_to_fix.overview: Set the Referrer-Policy header to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or 'no-referrer'.
how_to_fix.nginx: add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always;
how_to_fix.apache: Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
how_to_fix.express:
const helmet = require('helmet');
app.use(helmet.referrerPolicy({ policy: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' }));

example.good: Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin (sends origin only on cross-origin requests, full path only on same-origin).
example.bad: Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url (sends full URL and query params across all requests, even from HTTPS to HTTP).

common_mistakes: Using 'unsafe-url' or 'no-referrer-when-downgrade' which sends full paths and query strings across third-party domains.
Putting sensitive session tokens in GET query parameters instead of POST/Authorization headers, exacerbating referrer leakage.

status_meanings.PASS: Referrer-Policy is set to a secure value (e.g., strict-origin-when-cross-origin or no-referrer).
status_meanings.MISSING: Header is missing; browser defaults may vary across browser engines.
status_meanings.WARNING: Header is configured with an unsafe policy like 'unsafe-url'.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Policy is present with custom configuration needing privacy alignment check.

title: Permissions-Policy
short_description: Enables or disables sensitive browser hardware features and APIs (camera, microphone, geolocation, payment, USB) for the page and its iframes.
what_is_it: Permissions-Policy (previously called Feature-Policy) provides developers with granular control over which browser features and hardware APIs can be invoked by the current origin or delegated to embedded iframes.
why_it_matters: Modern web browsers expose powerful device capabilities: video cameras, microphones, accelerometer, gyroscope, geolocation, WebUSB, WebMIDI, and battery status. If your website does not need these capabilities, explicitly disabling them prevents third-party scripts or embedded ads from accessing user hardware without consent.
actual_problem: Third-party libraries, ad networks, or injected scripts can attempt to fingerprint users or access sensors unless the parent application explicitly revokes those permissions.
security_impact: Unauthorized sensor access, user hardware fingerprinting, battery status tracking, and privilege escalation within embedded frames.
how_to_check: Look for the 'Permissions-Policy' header and examine restricted features: 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()'.

how_to_fix.overview: Define a Permissions-Policy header turning off unused sensors and APIs.
how_to_fix.nginx: add_header Permissions-Policy "geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=(), payment=()" always;
how_to_fix.apache: Header always set Permissions-Policy "geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=(), payment=()"

example.good: Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(self)
example.bad: Header omitted, allowing embedded advertising iframes to request hardware permissions.

common_mistakes: Using the legacy 'Feature-Policy' header syntax instead of the modern structured 'Permissions-Policy' format.
Accidentally locking out legitimate features (e.g. disabling camera on a teleconferencing app).

status_meanings.PASS: Permissions-Policy is present and restricts sensitive device capabilities.
status_meanings.MISSING: Header is missing; browser applies default permissive feature policy.
status_meanings.WARNING: Legacy Feature-Policy header detected or syntax errors present.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Complex feature policy defined; review application feature needs.

title: Secure Cookie Flag
short_description: Ensures that HTTP cookies are only transmitted across encrypted HTTPS connections, never across unencrypted HTTP.
what_is_it: The 'Secure' attribute in the 'Set-Cookie' HTTP header instructs the user agent that the cookie must only be transmitted back to the server in requests encrypted with TLS (HTTPS). If the browser subsequently initiates an unencrypted HTTP request, the cookie is withheld.
why_it_matters: Session cookies and authentication tokens identify logged-in users. If a session cookie lacks the Secure flag, any unencrypted HTTP request to the same domain (e.g., loading an HTTP image or an accidental HTTP link click) causes the browser to send that cookie in cleartext over the network.
actual_problem: A passive network eavesdropper (e.g., sniffing Wi-Fi traffic) can capture the cleartext cookie and immediately impersonate the victim without needing their password.
security_impact: Session hijacking, credential theft, and persistent unauthorized account access.
how_to_check: Inspect 'Set-Cookie' response headers for the trailing '; Secure' flag directive.

how_to_fix.overview: Set the 'Secure' directive on all session, authentication, and sensitive state cookies in your application framework.
how_to_fix.nginx:
# If proxying cookies:
proxy_cookie_flags ~ secure;
how_to_fix.apache:
# In mod_headers
Header edit Set-Cookie ^(.*)$ "$1; Secure"
how_to_fix.flask:
# In Flask config:
app.config.update(
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True,
    REMEMBER_COOKIE_SECURE=True
)

example.good: Set-Cookie: session_id=xyz890; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
example.bad: Set-Cookie: session_id=xyz890; Path=/ (Transmitted over unencrypted HTTP).

common_mistakes: Setting Secure=True in development without local HTTPS, causing cookies not to be stored.
Protecting session cookies but omitting the Secure flag from CSRF or tracking cookies that also carry sensitive identifiers.

references.title: RFC 6265bis - Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism

status_meanings.PASS: All observed Set-Cookie directives include the 'Secure' attribute.
status_meanings.MISSING: One or more cookies are set without the 'Secure' attribute over HTTPS.
status_meanings.WARNING: Some cookies lack the Secure flag while others have it.
status_meanings.REVIEW: No cookies set on the inspected landing page; check authenticated endpoints.

title: HttpOnly Cookie Flag
short_description: Blocks client-side scripts (such as JavaScript) from accessing cookies via document.cookie, mitigating session theft via XSS.
what_is_it: The 'HttpOnly' attribute in the 'Set-Cookie' header ensures that the cookie is completely inaccessible to client-side scripts through APIs like 'document.cookie'. It is strictly used by the browser during HTTP requests to the server.
why_it_matters: When an attacker discovers a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability, their primary objective is typically to steal the victim's session cookie ('document.cookie') and exfiltrate it to an attacker-controlled server to take over the user's account.
actual_problem: If session cookies lack the HttpOnly attribute, any minor XSS flaw immediately escalates into full session hijacking.
security_impact: Immediate account takeover and session theft via exploited Cross-Site Scripting vulnerabilities.
how_to_check: Examine 'Set-Cookie' headers for '; HttpOnly'.

how_to_fix.overview: Configure your framework session manager to enforce HttpOnly on all authentication cookies.
how_to_fix.nginx: proxy_cookie_flags ~ httponly;
how_to_fix.apache: Header edit Set-Cookie ^(.*)$ "$1; HttpOnly"
how_to_fix.flask:
# In Flask config:
app.config.update(
    SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True,
    REMEMBER_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True
)

example.good: Set-Cookie: auth_token=abc1234; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict
example.bad: Set-Cookie: auth_token=abc1234; Path=/ (Exposed directly to document.cookie in JS).

common_mistakes: Believing HttpOnly prevents XSS itself (it mitigates cookie theft, but the attacker can still perform actions on behalf of the user via fetch).
Storing authentication tokens in localStorage or sessionStorage instead of HttpOnly cookies.

status_meanings.PASS: All observed cookies include the 'HttpOnly' flag.
status_meanings.MISSING: Session or sensitive cookies are set without 'HttpOnly'.
status_meanings.WARNING: Some non-essential cookies omit HttpOnly.
status_meanings.REVIEW: No cookies were issued during the passive scan of the landing page.

title: SameSite Cookie Attribute
short_description: Controls whether cookies are sent along with cross-site requests, providing a strong baseline defense against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF).
what_is_it: The 'SameSite' attribute in 'Set-Cookie' accepts three values: 'Strict' (never sent in cross-site requests), 'Lax' (sent on top-level safe GET navigations, but withheld on cross-site POST/PUT requests), and 'None' (sent on all cross-site requests, requires 'Secure').
why_it_matters: In a CSRF attack, a malicious website lures a victim into triggering an unauthorized state-changing request (e.g., submitting an invisible POST form to bank.com/transfer). Because browsers traditionally attached all cookies matching the target domain, the request executed authenticated.
actual_problem: Without SameSite=Lax or SameSite=Strict, browsers send authentication cookies in cross-origin requests by default, exposing users to CSRF.
security_impact: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), unauthorized form submissions, unintended transactions, and cross-site user tracking.
how_to_check: Inspect 'Set-Cookie' headers to verify that 'SameSite=Lax' or 'SameSite=Strict' is declared.

how_to_fix.overview: Set SameSite=Lax for normal user web sessions, or SameSite=Strict for high-security applications.
how_to_fix.nginx: proxy_cookie_flags ~ "SameSite=Lax";
how_to_fix.apache: Header edit Set-Cookie ^(.*)$ "$1; SameSite=Lax"
how_to_fix.flask:
# In Flask config:
app.config.update(
    SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax'
)

example.good: Set-Cookie: session=sess_998; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
example.bad: Set-Cookie: session=sess_998; Path=/; SameSite=None (without anti-CSRF tokens).

common_mistakes: Setting SameSite=None without the Secure attribute (rejected by modern browsers).
Assuming SameSite=Lax completely replaces CSRF tokens (GET requests can still leak or trigger unintended idempotent side-effects if improperly designed).

references.title: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

status_meanings.PASS: Observed cookies have SameSite set to Lax or Strict.
status_meanings.MISSING: Cookies omit the SameSite attribute.
status_meanings.WARNING: SameSite is set to None, allowing cross-site cookie transmission.
status_meanings.REVIEW: No cookies observed on initial response.

title: CORS Configuration (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)
short_description: Validates that the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is strictly configured and does not unsafely expose private APIs to arbitrary origins.
what_is_it: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a browser mechanism that relaxes the Same-Origin Policy (SOP). The server sends headers like 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' and 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials' to specify which foreign origins are permitted to read its responses.
why_it_matters: If an internal API or sensitive web service sets 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' or dynamically echoes back the incoming 'Origin' header while enabling credentials ('Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true'), any malicious website visited by an authenticated user can perform XMLHttpRequest/fetch calls to read their private account data.
actual_problem: Misconfigured CORS headers bypass the fundamental browser security boundary, permitting unauthorized external origins to read authenticated responses.
security_impact: Data exfiltration, theft of sensitive JSON/XML customer data, API abuse, and full bypass of the Same-Origin Policy.
how_to_check: Send an HTTP request with an arbitrary Origin header (e.g. 'Origin: https://evil.com') and check if the server returns 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' or echoes 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com' alongside 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true'.

how_to_fix.overview: Do not use wildcard '*' on authenticated endpoints. Validate incoming Origin headers against an explicit, static whitelist of trusted origins.
how_to_fix.apache:
SetEnvIf Origin "^https://(app|dashboard)\.example\.com$" CORS_ALLOW=$0
Header always set Access-Control-Allow-Origin %{CORS_ALLOW}e env=CORS_ALLOW
how_to_fix.flask:
from flask_cors import CORS
# Whitelist specific origins
CORS(app, origins=["https://trusted.example.com"], supports_credentials=True)

example.good: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://trusted-partner.example.com
example.bad: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (on private user profile API) or echoing arbitrary Origin with credentials: true.

common_mistakes: Blindly echoing the request's Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
Using insecure regex matching like /example.com/ which matches attacker-owned domains like 'example.com.evil.com' or 'evilexample.com'.
Enabling 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true' with a wildcard origin (modern browsers block this, but flawed custom proxies can cause issues).

status_meanings.PASS: CORS headers are absent (standard SOP applies) or restricted to specific trusted origins.
status_meanings.MISSING: N/A (Absence of CORS header is secure by default as SOP is enforced).
status_meanings.WARNING: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is configured on the scanned endpoint.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Custom CORS configuration detected; verify whitelist validation logic.

title: Server Information Disclosure
short_description: Checks if the server leaks unnecessary software names, exact version numbers, or operating system details via response headers.
what_is_it: Web servers and backend frameworks frequently broadcast their identity via default HTTP headers such as 'Server', 'X-Powered-By', 'X-AspNet-Version', and 'X-Runtime'.
why_it_matters: When attackers perform reconnaissance on a target, discovering exact versions (e.g. 'Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu)', 'PHP/7.2.24', 'Express') allows them to search CVE databases (like NIST NVD or Exploit-DB) for specific unpatched vulnerabilities and exploits.
actual_problem: Broadcasting software versions aids automated vulnerability scanners in identifying vulnerable software versions without requiring active exploitation.
security_impact: Aids targeted exploitation, exposes unpatched CVEs, and simplifies attacker reconnaissance.
how_to_check: Examine response headers for 'Server' and 'X-Powered-By'.

how_to_fix.overview: Strip or generalize the Server header and completely remove X-Powered-By.
how_to_fix.nginx:
# In http block of nginx.conf
server_tokens off;
how_to_fix.apache:
# In apache2.conf
ServerTokens Prod
ServerSignature Off
how_to_fix.flask:
# Flask does not emit X-Powered-By by default. In Werkzeug/Gunicorn, override Server header:
# gunicorn --server-name 'webserver' ...

example.good: Server: cloudflare (generic) or header completely suppressed; X-Powered-By absent.
example.bad: Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu) mod_ssl/2.4.41 OpenSSL/1.1.1f / X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3

common_mistakes: Assuming hiding the Server header is sufficient security on its own ('security through obscurity'). The software must still be kept updated.
Forgetting framework headers like X-Powered-By or X-AspNet-Version.

references.title: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

status_meanings.PASS: Server tokens are suppressed or generic (e.g., no detailed version numbers).
status_meanings.MISSING: N/A
status_meanings.WARNING: Detailed software name and specific version numbers are leaked in headers.
status_meanings.REVIEW: A generic Server header is present; verify internal version disclosure policies.

title: Cache-Control Security
short_description: Ensures sensitive responses are protected from unauthorized storage in shared proxies, browser caches, and intermediate CDNs.
what_is_it: The 'Cache-Control' header manages how, where, and for how long HTTP responses can be stored by client browsers and intermediate proxy caches. Directives like 'no-store', 'no-cache', and 'private' control caching behavior.
why_it_matters: When a user logs into a sensitive portal (such as a patient health record or banking dashboard), responses contain private information. If the server does not specify 'Cache-Control: no-store, private', the data can be written to disk cache or cached in intermediate shared proxy caches.
actual_problem: Subsequent users on a shared workstation or users accessing browser history can inspect cached personal documents and session data without re-authenticating.
security_impact: Unauthorized exposure of cached PII and sensitive transactions on shared workstations or via proxy cache deception.
how_to_check: Inspect 'Cache-Control' and 'Pragma' headers on sensitive endpoints.

how_to_fix.overview: Apply 'Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=0' on all sensitive dynamic responses.
how_to_fix.apache:
<LocationMatch "^/api/">
    Header set Cache-Control "no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0"
    Header set Pragma "no-cache"
</LocationMatch>

example.good: Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=0 (for authenticated or personal data endpoints)
example.bad: Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 (for sensitive account settings).

common_mistakes: Using 'no-cache' instead of 'no-store' (no-cache still stores the response on disk; it merely validates before reuse).
Accidentally disabling caching on static immutable assets (CSS/JS/images), hurting performance.

status_meanings.PASS: Cache-Control header is appropriately configured.
status_meanings.MISSING: Cache-Control header is absent on response.
status_meanings.WARNING: Potentially sensitive endpoint marked as public cacheable.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Public caching detected; standard for landing pages, review authenticated routes.

title: DNS Security & CAA Records
short_description: Evaluates DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) and email authentication records to prevent fraudulent certificate issuance and spoofing.
what_is_it: DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA, RFC 8659) is a DNS resource record allowing domain owners to specify which Certificate Authorities (CAs) are legally permitted to issue SSL/TLS certificates for their domain.
why_it_matters: Before issuing any public TLS certificate, public CAs are mandated by the CA/Browser Forum to query the domain's CAA records. If an attacker compromises an obscure CA or tricks a validation system, a CAA record prevents unauthorized CAs from generating rogue certificates.
actual_problem: Without CAA records, any of the hundreds of publicly trusted root CAs worldwide can issue a certificate for your domain if an attacker deceives their domain validation checks.
security_impact: Man-in-the-Middle interception using fraudulent certificates issued by rogue or compromised Certificate Authorities.
how_to_check: Perform a DNS query for the CAA record type: 'dig CAA example.com +short' or 'nslookup -type=CAA example.com'.

how_to_fix.overview: Add CAA records in your DNS management zone specifying your chosen Certificate Authorities (e.g. Let's Encrypt, DigiCert).
how_to_fix.nginx:
# CAA is configured in DNS, not in Nginx. Add record to your DNS zone file:
# example.com. IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
# example.com. IN CAA 0 iodef "mailto:security@example.com"
how_to_fix.apache: # Configured in DNS zone manager (Cloudflare, Route53, BIND).
how_to_fix.flask: # Managed at the DNS registrar / nameserver level.
how_to_fix.express: # Managed at the DNS registrar / nameserver level.

example.good: example.com. IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
example.bad: No CAA records configured; any public CA in the world can issue certificates.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to include 'issuewild' if wildcard certificates are required (*.example.com).
Configuring CAA on the apex domain but using a DNS provider that does not resolve records for subdomains.

status_meanings.PASS: Valid CAA records found restricting certificate issuance to authorized CAs.
status_meanings.MISSING: No CAA records configured in DNS; any public CA may issue certificates.
status_meanings.WARNING: CAA record syntax issues or restricted policies without emergency alert iodef.
status_meanings.REVIEW: DNS lookup encountered provider throttling or non-standard zone delegation.

title: Certificate Validity & Trust Chain
short_description: Validates the digital certificate chain of trust, verifying that the certificate is signed by a recognized CA and matches the scanned hostname.
what_is_it: A digital certificate binds a cryptographic public key to a specific domain name. The browser verifies the cryptographic signature chain through intermediate authorities back to an embedded trusted Root Certificate Authority in the OS/browser trust store.
why_it_matters: If a certificate is self-signed, untrusted, revoked, or issued for a different hostname, browsers immediately display a security warning screen ('Your connection is not private'). Most users will abandon the site, and those who bypass it become vulnerable to interception.
actual_problem: Host mismatch (Common Name or Subject Alternative Names don't match the URL), broken intermediate certificate chains, or expired root certificates.
security_impact: Complete breakdown of browser trust, immediate deterrence of visitors, or exposure to Man-in-the-Middle credential interception.
how_to_check: Examine the certificate details in your browser or run: 'openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com'.

how_to_fix.overview: Deploy a certificate signed by a publicly trusted CA and ensure the complete intermediate bundle ('fullchain.pem') is configured on the web server.
how_to_fix.apache:
SSLCertificateFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/cert.pem
SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem
SSLCertificateChainFile /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/chain.pem
how_to_fix.flask: # In production, terminate SSL at Nginx/Cloudflare.

example.good: Certificate issued by 'Let's Encrypt / R3', matches domain 'example.com', valid chain of trust.
example.bad: Self-signed certificate, hostname mismatch ('example.net' used on 'example.com'), or missing intermediate certificate.

common_mistakes: Serving only the leaf certificate without intermediate CA certificates, causing mobile devices to fail verification.
Forgetting to include both apex domain ('example.com') and www ('www.example.com') in the Subject Alternative Names (SANs).

references.title: RFC 5280 - Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile

status_meanings.PASS: Certificate is valid, trusted, matches hostname, and verified by standard trust store.
status_meanings.MISSING: No SSL/TLS certificate found on port 443.
status_meanings.WARNING: Certificate chain is incomplete (missing intermediates) or SAN mismatch.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Certificate is self-signed or from an internal private PKI.

title: Certificate Expiry & Renewal Horizon
short_description: Monitors the remaining lifespan of the SSL/TLS certificate to prevent service disruptions and browser security blocking.
what_is_it: All SSL/TLS certificates have strict start ('notBefore') and expiration ('notAfter') timestamps. Modern industry rules (CA/B Forum) limit certificate validity to a maximum of 398 days (and standard Let's Encrypt certs last 90 days).
why_it_matters: When a certificate reaches its expiration timestamp, browsers instantly treat all subsequent HTTPS requests as untrusted, blocking user access with a severe warning ('SEC_ERROR_EXPIRED_CERTIFICATE'). Web APIs immediately fail.
actual_problem: Failure to automate renewal leads to unexpected website outages, customer panic, and severe business disruption.
security_impact: Full denial of service for all users, broken API client integrations, and damage to brand reputation.
how_to_check: Check expiration via OpenSSL: 'echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates'.

how_to_fix.overview: Implement automated renewal jobs using Certbot, ACME clients, or managed cloud certificate managers (AWS ACM, Cloudflare).
how_to_fix.nginx:
# Test automated certbot renewal cron / systemd timer:
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
how_to_fix.apache:
# Enable certbot timer
sudo systemctl status certbot.timer
how_to_fix.flask: # Handle certificate automation at the reverse proxy layer.
how_to_fix.express: # Handle certificate automation at the reverse proxy or hosting provider.

example.good: Certificate expires in 74 days; automated renewal job scheduled for day 30.
example.bad: Certificate expires in 3 days, or already expired 12 hours ago.

common_mistakes: Relying on manual calendar reminders instead of automated ACME cron/systemd renewal timers.
Renewing the certificate on disk but failing to reload the web server daemon (e.g. nginx -s reload), so the old certificate remains in memory.

status_meanings.PASS: Certificate has more than 30 days of validity remaining.
status_meanings.MISSING: Certificate has already expired.
status_meanings.WARNING: Certificate expires soon (within 30 days); renewal recommended immediately.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Certificate validity duration is non-standard.

title: Mixed Content Prevention
short_description: Ensures that a site delivered over HTTPS does not load sub-resources (scripts, styles, images, iframes) over unencrypted HTTP.
what_is_it: Mixed content occurs when an initial HTML document is loaded securely over HTTPS, but child resources (such as images, scripts, stylesheets, audio, video, or iframes) are fetched over insecure HTTP.
why_it_matters: Active mixed content (scripts, stylesheets, iframes) allows a network attacker to modify the insecure resource in transit and execute arbitrary code inside the secure parent page, completely undermining the protection HTTPS provides.
actual_problem: Modern browsers automatically block active mixed content, which breaks site functionality. Passive mixed content (e.g. images) degrades the browser's security indicator from a secure padlock to a warning.
security_impact: Man-in-the-Middle script execution on an otherwise HTTPS page, broken site layout, and loss of user trust.
how_to_check: Inspect browser developer console for 'Mixed Content:' warnings or verify that the CSP header includes 'upgrade-insecure-requests'.

how_to_fix.overview: Update all internal hardcoded asset URLs from 'http://' to 'https://' or use relative paths ('/static/css/style.css'). Add the 'upgrade-insecure-requests' CSP directive.
how_to_fix.nginx:
# In your CSP header:
add_header Content-Security-Policy "upgrade-insecure-requests;" always;
how_to_fix.apache: Header always set Content-Security-Policy "upgrade-insecure-requests;"

example.good: <script src="https://cdn.example.com/app.js"></script> or relative src="/js/app.js"
example.bad: <script src="http://cdn.example.com/app.js"></script> inside an HTTPS page.

common_mistakes: Hardcoding 'http://' URLs into database CMS entries (e.g. WordPress media links).
Failing to check third-party embedded widgets or analytics scripts.

references.title: Google Web Fundamentals: What is Mixed Content?

status_meanings.PASS: Page is served over HTTPS and includes 'upgrade-insecure-requests' CSP directive.
status_meanings.MISSING: Insecure HTTP resource links detected within the HTTPS landing page.
status_meanings.WARNING: HTTPS active but no automatic upgrade directive declared.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Passive scan verified response structure; perform deep-crawl for dynamic assets.

title: Redirect Security & HTTP-to-HTTPS Redirection
short_description: Validates that initial unencrypted HTTP traffic is seamlessly and safely redirected to HTTPS using permanent 301/308 redirects.
what_is_it: Redirect security verifies that when a user requests the insecure HTTP version of a website (port 80), the server immediately issues an HTTP 301 (Moved Permanently) or 308 (Permanent Redirect) response pointing directly to the equivalent HTTPS URL (port 443).
why_it_matters: If a website serves content simultaneously over both HTTP and HTTPS without redirecting, users who type the domain without 'https://' will continue browsing unencrypted. Furthermore, intermediate redirect chains that hop across different unencrypted domains expose requests to interception.
actual_problem: Failing to redirect plaintext HTTP requests to HTTPS leaves visitors unencrypted by default. Multi-hop redirects also slow down page load times and increase the attack surface.
security_impact: Exposure to eavesdropping on the initial connection and loss of transport security guarantees.
how_to_check: Run 'curl -IL http://example.com' and observe the status codes and Location headers in the redirect chain.

how_to_fix.overview: Configure a dedicated HTTP port 80 server block that returns a 301 redirect to the exact same HTTPS URL.
how_to_fix.apache:
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    Redirect permanent / https://example.com/
</VirtualHost>
how_to_fix.flask:
# In production, handle redirection at Nginx/Load Balancer. In Flask with Talisman:
# from flask_talisman import Talisman
# Talisman(app, force_https=True)

example.good: http://example.com -> [301 Moved Permanently] -> https://example.com -> [200 OK]
example.bad: http://example.com -> [200 OK] (serving unencrypted website directly on port 80).

common_mistakes: Using a 302 temporary redirect instead of a 301/308 permanent redirect (search engines and browsers won't cache it).
Redirecting from HTTP on domain A to HTTP on domain B before finally redirecting to HTTPS.

references.title: Google Search Central: Secure your site with HTTPS

status_meanings.PASS: Plaintext HTTP cleanly redirects to HTTPS with a 301/308 status code.
status_meanings.MISSING: HTTP port 80 serves content in plaintext without redirecting to HTTPS.
status_meanings.WARNING: HTTP redirects via 302 (temporary) or has intermediate insecure hops.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Direct connection on target URL; initial HTTP redirect behavior not observed.

title: Security Headers Overall Configuration
short_description: Synthesizes the defense-in-depth posture of the target server by evaluating the combined coverage of modern security headers.
what_is_it: Modern web defense relies on defense-in-depth. No single security header is an absolute panacea. A resilient website combines HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy to form a comprehensive browser-side defensive perimeter.
why_it_matters: Leaving gaps in your header configuration leaves doors open to specific attack classes: missing XFO allows clickjacking; missing CSP allows XSS; missing HSTS allows SSL-stripping. Implementing them harmoniously ensures that even if one application layer has a bug, the browser will suppress exploitation.
actual_problem: Fragmented or piecemeal security header adoption where developers deploy one or two headers while neglecting the rest.
security_impact: Incomplete defense-in-depth leaving application vulnerabilities exploitable at the client layer.
how_to_check: Perform a comprehensive header inspection and tally how many core headers (HSTS, CSP, XFO, XCTO, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) are actively returned.

how_to_fix.overview: Adopt a centralized security headers configuration snippet in your reverse proxy or web application framework.
how_to_fix.apache:
# In apache VirtualHost:
Header always set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"
Header always set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; object-src 'none';"
how_to_fix.flask:
# In Flask:
@app.after_request
def apply_security_headers(res):
    res.headers['X-Content-Type-Options'] = 'nosniff'
    res.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = 'DENY'
    res.headers['Referrer-Policy'] = 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin'
    res.headers['Strict-Transport-Security'] = 'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains'
    return res
how_to_fix.express:
const helmet = require('helmet');
app.use(helmet()); // Enables all recommended security headers automatically

example.good: Server returns HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy.
example.bad: Server returns zero security headers, relying entirely on default browser heuristics.

common_mistakes: Adding headers in web framework code but having them stripped by a misconfigured caching proxy or CDN.
Copy-pasting overly restrictive CSP directives that break third-party payment gateways or fonts.

status_meanings.PASS: Optimal coverage: >= 5 of 6 essential defense-in-depth headers are actively deployed.
status_meanings.MISSING: Minimal coverage: Fewer than 2 security headers are configured.
status_meanings.WARNING: Moderate coverage: 2 to 4 security headers configured; key defenses still missing.
status_meanings.REVIEW: Headers configured but inconsistent across different response status codes.
